title: The Rudd Concession at Bulawayo
subtitle: Lobengula's kraal, Matabeleland, and the road to the British South Africa Company charter, 1888–1889 (with the 1893 war as epilogue)
intro: In 1888 the kingdom of the amaNdebele (Ndebele, called 'Matabele' in the English record), ruled from Bulawayo by Lobengula Khumalo, became the target of a crowd of concession-seekers. Gold had been found on the Witwatersrand in 1886, and men in Kimberley and London believed the high country to the north, which the amaNdebele raided and claimed, might hold a second Rand. In February 1888 the missionary-turned-official John Smith Moffat obtained the king's mark on a short treaty of friendship. Under it Lobengula undertook not to deal with any foreign power over his territory without the British High Commissioner's sanction. Eight months later, on 30 October 1888, Charles Rudd, Rochfort Maguire and Francis 'Matabele' Thompson, acting for Cecil Rhodes, obtained his mark on a single page granting them 'complete and exclusive charge over all metals and minerals' in his kingdoms. In return they promised £100 every lunar month, 1,000 Martini-Henry rifles with 100,000 rounds, and a steamboat on the Zambezi or £500 in its place.

This chapter sets the documents of that one negotiation side by side. They are: the concession text and the missionary Charles Helm's certificate that he had explained it; Rudd's journal of the journey; Thompson's later autobiography; the letters and public notices Lobengula dictated to white scribes at Bulawayo; the reported words of his two senior izinduna (councillors), Mshete and Babayane, who went to Windsor in March 1889; the letter written in Queen Victoria's name in reply; the questions put in the House of Commons; and later recollections from people who were at Bulawayo in 1889. The record is mostly letters, notices, parliamentary answers and memoirs written long afterwards rather than diaries, and the form tags say so. Almost nothing survives in the amaNdebele's own hand. Lobengula's letters were written in English by missionaries, traders or rival concession-seekers, each with an interest of his own, and his councillors' words reached London through interpreters.

The central dispute is the gap between the page and the conversation. The written text grants minerals, the power to do what was needed to win them, and the right to exclude rival concession-seekers. It sets no limit on how many men might come. Helm later confirmed that Rudd had also made spoken promises that never went into the document: that no more than ten white men would come to dig, that they would not dig near towns, and that they would obey the laws of the country. Lobengula's letters of 1889 say he had been told one thing and had signed another. The grantees and their supporters held that the king and his council had had the paper explained and had accepted its terms with the rifles in view. The chapter sets these positions out without a verdict.

The concession became the legal foundation of the British South Africa Company, whose royal charter was granted on 29 October 1889. On the way there it produced a public repudiation, a diplomatic mission to the Queen, a Commons debate about arms and monopoly, and a political crisis at Bulawayo. In that crisis the king's senior councillor Lotshe Hlabangana, who had advised accepting the rifles, was put to death with members of his household in September 1889. The epilogue is brief. In 1890 the Company's Pioneer Column occupied Mashonaland. In 1893 the Company made war on the amaNdebele kingdom. Bulawayo was burned and abandoned in November, and Lobengula died in the north in January 1894.

The vantage points run from the king's own enclosure, through the missionary-interpreter who stood between the parties, out to Kimberley, Cape Town, Westminster and Windsor, and on to the 1930s, when an amaNdebele veteran told his story to a British scholar. Read together, they show how few hands the words passed through, and how much depended on who was holding the pen.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian. The concession's money terms were set by the lunar month (£100 'on the first day of every lunar month'), which is why Hansard gave the annual value variously as £1,200 and £1,260. Secondary sources disagree on when the izinduna left Bulawayo with Maund: dates from 1 November to mid-December 1888 appear. Their departure is therefore entered by month and marked approximate.
vantage_key: 0 = a principal at the king's council or a signatory (the king, the grantees, his envoys); 1 = on the scene at Bulawayo as interpreter, official or visitor; 2 = in the same region (Kimberley, Cape Town, the Bechuanaland border) handling the papers; 3 = in Britain, in Parliament or at court, reading reports; 4 = recalling the events decades later.

eyes.name: Lobengula Khumalo
eyes.role: King (inkosi) of the amaNdebele since 1870, then in his early forties
eyes.where: His towns at Bulawayo (Gubulawayo) and the royal kraal at Umvutcha, north of the modern city
eyes.form: dictated letters and public notices (written in English by missionaries, traders and concession agents)
eyes.authenticity: No document in his own hand exists. His notices and letters were taken down in English by white residents of Bulawayo, some of them rivals of the Rudd party, and were printed in South African newspapers and in the Colonial Office Blue Book C.5918 (1890). The letter of 23 April 1889 is C.5918, enclosure in no. 101. Each must be read as his words as rendered by a particular scribe.
eyes.bio: Son of Mzilikazi, founder of the kingdom, Lobengula ruled a powerful state, and in 1888 he was managing rival British, Boer and Portuguese approaches at once. He put his mark to the Moffat treaty and then the Rudd Concession. Within weeks he was disputing what the latter meant. He sent envoys to the Queen, published a suspension notice, and dictated letters saying the paper contained neither his words nor those of the men who got it.

sources.title: Lobengula to Queen Victoria, 23 April 1889, as reprinted (Macmillan 'Viewpoints' reader, from E. D. Morel, The Black Man's Burden, 1920)
E. D. Morel, The Black Man's Burden (1920), p. 34 (Wikisource page scan mirror)
R. Cary, 'Jameson and Lobengula, 1889–90' (University of Zimbabwe repository)

eyes.name: Charles Dunell Rudd
eyes.role: Kimberley diamond magnate, Rhodes's business partner in De Beers and Gold Fields of South Africa; leader of the concession party, aged 44
eyes.where: Travelled Kimberley to Umvutcha and back

waypoints.label: Shoshong (Khama's capital), held up en route

eyes.authenticity: His journal of the concession journey was first published in 1949 in 'Gold and the Gospel in Mashonaland, 1888' (Oppenheimer Series no. 4, Chatto & Windus), together with Bishop Knight-Bruce's journals. It is quoted here only by digest.
eyes.bio: Rudd was the senior partner on the journey and the man whose name the concession bears. His journal gives the grantees' account of the signing: the king seated on an old brandy case in the goat kraal, uneasy, saying for half an hour that his promise was enough, then making his mark. His return through the desert almost killed him.

sources.title: Gold and the Gospel in Mashonaland, 1888 (1949), catalogue record
Zimbabwe Field Guide: Were Lobengula and the amaNdebele tricked by the Rudd Concession?

eyes.name: Francis Robert 'Matabele' Thompson
eyes.role: Cape-born farmer and Rhodes's agent, the party member who spoke isiZulu/isiNdebele; aged 31
eyes.authenticity: His recollections were edited by Nancy Rouillard as 'Matabele Thompson: An Autobiography' (first published 1936; reissued in the Books of Rhodesia series, Bulawayo, 1977). Written decades after the events and in places disputed by other witnesses such as Ivon Fry, especially on Lotshe's death and Thompson's flight. Digest only.
eyes.bio: Thompson was the party's go-between with the izinduna. By his own account he promised gifts to Lotshe and Sikombo for their help, and he held a private talk with the king just before the signing. He stayed on at Bulawayo to deliver payments and rifles. Interrogated by the izinduna in March 1889, he fled the country after Lotshe was killed in September.

sources.title: Zimbabwe Field Guide: Matabele Thompson; his role in the Rudd Concession

eyes.name: Rev. Charles Daniel Helm
eyes.role: London Missionary Society missionary at Hope Fountain, near Bulawayo, since 1875; interpreter and witness to the concession
eyes.where: Hope Fountain mission, about 12 miles from Bulawayo
eyes.form: signed certificate; dated letters to the LMS
eyes.authenticity: His endorsement is printed with the concession text. His letters to the LMS directors in London are in the LMS archives at SOAS (for example, to Wardlaw Thompson, 20 December 1889, cited by Cary). Later historians have criticised his role, as some contemporaries did. He was charged with misrepresenting the terms and with being in the grantees' pay; he maintained he had explained the document fully.
eyes.bio: Helm was the one person on the ground who could read the English and speak to the king, so the concession's legitimacy rested on his certificate. He also later confirmed that Rudd had made spoken promises that were not written in. Early in 1889 he read the real text to the king to counter a trader's embellished version. That pleased neither the concession's critics nor its promoters.

sources.title: SAHO: text of the Rudd Concession with Helm's endorsement
R. Cary, 'Jameson and Lobengula, 1889–90'

eyes.name: John Smith Moffat
eyes.role: Former LMS missionary, son of Robert Moffat; Assistant Commissioner in Bechuanaland posted to Bulawayo, aged 52
eyes.vantage_label: the Queen's officer at the king's town
eyes.authenticity: The 11 February 1888 treaty bears Lobengula's mark, witnessed before Moffat, and was ratified by Robinson on 25 April 1888. His official letters are in the Blue Books (e.g. Moffat to Shippard, 28 August 1889, C.5918 no. 131). A memoir with letters by his son R. U. Moffat appeared in 1921.
eyes.bio: Moffat traded on the trust his father had built with Mzilikazi's house to secure the treaty that closed Matabeleland to other powers. He was later uneasy about how the Company dealt with the king and eventually broke with Rhodes. His position shows the Crown's interest, which differed from the Company's while running alongside it.

sources.title: Zimbabwe Field Guide (Moffat treaty, witnesses and ratification)
SAHO: John Smith Moffat

eyes.name: Sir Sidney Godolphin Alexander Shippard
eyes.role: Administrator of British Bechuanaland and Deputy Commissioner for the Protectorate
eyes.authenticity: His reports are in the Colonial Office correspondence printed as Blue Books. His whereabouts at the signing are recorded in the Under-Secretary's answer in the Commons, 25 February 1889. His reported encouragement of the king in Rhodes's favour comes from secondary accounts and from later recollection.
eyes.bio: Shippard rode up to Bulawayo in mid-October 1888 with Hamilton Goold-Adams and an escort of sixteen Bechuanaland Border Police, a fortnight before the signing. Historians generally hold that his visit favoured Rhodes's party. Officially, London told Parliament he had been a hundred miles away and knew nothing of the negotiations.

sources.title: Hansard, HC Deb 25 February 1889: South Africa, the De Beers mine

eyes.name: Sir Hercules Robinson
eyes.role: Governor of the Cape Colony and High Commissioner for South Africa
eyes.authenticity: His dispatches to the Colonial Office (e.g. 5 December 1888 on the concession; telegram of 2 February 1889 on the envoys) are in the Blue Books and cited by Keppel-Jones and others. Parliament heard his view summarised by the Under-Secretary on 25 February 1889.
eyes.bio: Robinson ratified the Moffat treaty and wrote the letter that helped Rudd's party past Khama. He then reported favourably on the concession as public policy, a view Parliament was told he held without having formally approved it. He retired in May 1889 and was succeeded by Sir Henry Loch.

sources.title: Hansard, HC Deb 25 February 1889
Zimbabwe Field Guide: Why Lobengula sent envoys to Queen Victoria

eyes.name: Edward Arthur Maund
eyes.role: Former army officer, agent of the London-based Exploring Company syndicate; rival concession-seeker
eyes.where: Bulawayo, then escorting the envoys to London
eyes.authenticity: His letters (e.g. to the Colonial Office, 7 August 1889) and papers are cited by Parsons, Keppel-Jones and Rotberg. He took down in English the letter the envoys carried, so that text passed through a man with a competing interest.
eyes.bio: Maund reached Bulawayo about three weeks after Rudd, too late. He became the escort of the king's mission to the Queen and interpreted at the Colonial Office. In April 1889, once Rhodes had bought out his syndicate's interest, Rhodes instructed Maguire and Thompson to work with him.

sources.title: M. Plaut, 'Lobenguela's izinduna', Quarterly Bulletin of the National Library of South Africa (2016), via SAHO

eyes.name: Mshete (Mtshede ka Mabuyana) and Babayane (Babiyane ka Masuku)
eyes.role: Senior izinduna of Lobengula, about 60 and 75 years old, sent as his envoys to Queen Victoria
eyes.where: Bulawayo to Cape Town, London and Windsor, and back
eyes.form: reported speech (as interpreted) and later recollection
eyes.language: isiNdebele, interpreted by Maund and Johan Colenbrander
eyes.authenticity: No writing of their own survives. What they said reached the record through interpreters, the British press, and the Colonial Under-Secretary's answers in the Commons. Babayane's later account of London, told at Rhodes's camp in 1896, survives only as reported by others. Popular modern accounts sometimes name Lotshe as an envoy; the contemporary record names Mshete and Babayane.
eyes.bio: The king's letter called the izinduna 'his eyes', and they were sent to find out whether the Queen existed and to ask her advice. In London they met the Colonial Secretary and the Queen, breakfasted with the Aborigines' Protection Society, and were shown the army at Aldershot and the guns at Woolwich. They came home in August 1889 with a letter advising caution and a gold-looking chain.

sources.title: M. Plaut, 'Lobenguela's izinduna' (2016), via SAHO
Zimbabwe Field Guide: Why Lobengula sent envoys to Queen Victoria
Zimbabwe Field Guide: Two of Lobengula's relics

eyes.name: Queen Victoria (with Lord Knutsford, Colonial Secretary)
eyes.role: Queen of the United Kingdom, aged 69; her reply was drafted and signed for her by the Colonial Office
eyes.vantage_label: the Queen the envoys came to see
eyes.form: letter (written in her name by the Colonial Office); inscribed gift
eyes.authenticity: The reply of 26 March 1889 was issued by Lord Knutsford at the Colonial Office in the Queen's name and printed in the Blue Book correspondence; it is quotable. The gift chain, inscribed and dated March 1889, survives in a South African museum collection. The Queen's private journal for these days is held in the Royal Archives and is not drawn on here.
eyes.bio: The Queen received the two izinduna in St George's Hall, Windsor, on 2 March 1889, with fifty Life Guards in attendance. The reply sent in her name became the most quoted document of the episode. It told the king to be careful with concessions, in a cattle image he could not mistake, and also to trust the High Commissioner, who had backed Rudd.

sources.title: Zimbabwe Field Guide: Why Lobengula sent envoys (text of the 26 March 1889 reply)
Zimbabwe Field Guide: Two of Lobengula's relics (the inscribed chain)

eyes.name: Baron Henry de Worms
eyes.role: Conservative MP and Under-Secretary of State for the Colonies, answering for the government in the Commons
eyes.authenticity: Hansard's record of Commons questions and answers, 25 February to 2 April 1889, as digitised by the UK Parliament. The questioners included Charles Bradlaugh, Joseph Chamberlain, Henry Labouchere and Alexander M'Arthur.
eyes.bio: Week after week, de Worms had to explain a concession that London had neither approved nor forbidden. MPs pressed him on the rifles, the monopoly, and the size of the grant, which Chamberlain called 'the size of Italy'. They also pressed him on whether the king had disowned it. His answers trace the government's move from 'no opinion' to a plan to bring all concessions under one control, which became the chartered company.

sources.title: HC Deb 25 February 1889
HC Deb 11 March 1889
HC Deb 15 March 1889
HC Deb 26 March 1889
HC Deb 2 April 1889

eyes.name: H. Vaughn-Williams
eyes.role: Nineteen-year-old visitor from Britain (later a lieutenant-colonel) staying at the royal kraal with his brother Arthur
eyes.authenticity: Published as 'A Visit to Lobengula in 1889' (Shuter and Shooter, Pietermaritzburg, 1947), some 57 years after the events. Digest only. Details of the September 1889 killings come from his recollection and should be read with that distance in mind.
eyes.bio: Vaughn-Williams arrived as a teenager in August 1889 and stayed nearly three months, so he was at the kraal through the September crisis. He remembered the king as commanding and dignified. His account is a witness's memory, set down very late, of Lotshe's death and the king's reaction to Thompson's flight.

sources.title: Zimbabwe Field Guide: The King's Kraal, Umvutcha (from Vaughn-Williams, 1947)
Zimbabwe Field Guide: Vaughn-Williams recollections

eyes.name: Ivon Fry
eyes.role: Son of J. L. Fry, a De Beers man sent earlier by Rhodes to seek a concession; stayed at Bulawayo as Rhodes's agent
eyes.authenticity: Reminiscences taken down by the Bulawayo Chronicle journalist Foster Windram in September–October 1938, when Fry was 74; typescript held by the Windram family and summarised online. They contradict Thompson's memoir on several points. Digest only.
eyes.bio: Fry's father had sought a concession from Lobengula before Rudd and died in Kimberley as the Rudd party returned. Fry's memories show a crowded field of rival claims and traders' hostility to the concession. He also gives a version of Lotshe's fall that differs from Thompson's.

sources.title: Zimbabwe Field Guide: Ivon Fry's reminiscences of Bulawayo and Lobengula in 1888–89

eyes.name: Ndansi Kumalo
eyes.role: Young amaNdebele man of fighting age in 1893; in the 1930s, cast as Lobengula in a British film about Rhodes
eyes.vantage_label: an amaNdebele witness of the war, telling it in the 1930s
eyes.language: isiNdebele, through an interpreter, into English
eyes.authenticity: His narrative was taken down by Margery Perham and published in 'Ten Africans' (Faber and Faber, 1936). It is a later, interpreted account. Digest only.
eyes.bio: Ndansi Kumalo gives one of the few published amaNdebele narratives of how the arrangements of 1888–89 ended. He insisted the king had wanted no war and had been under the Queen's protection. He tells of the Company's columns entering Bulawayo, the burning of the king's enclosure, the loss of the cattle and the surrender of arms.

sources.title: Ndansi Kumalo, account of the British incursion (from Perham, Ten Africans, 1936), Macmillan sources reader

entries.headline: A short treaty of friendship, and a door quietly closed
entries.digest: Moffat obtained the king's mark on a brief treaty. In it Lobengula promised peace with Britain and undertook not to enter into any correspondence or treaty with a foreign power, or to cede any part of his country, without the High Commissioner's sanction. The traders W. Graham and G. B. van Wyk witnessed it. Read in Cape Town, it placed Matabeleland in a British sphere. Read at Bulawayo, it was a pledge of friendship.
entries.source_note: Treaty date and witnesses as given in Zimbabwe Field Guide, 'Were Lobengula and the amaNdebele tricked by the Rudd concession?' (citing Warhurst, Rhodesiana Publication 29).

entries.headline: The High Commissioner ratifies the Moffat treaty
entries.digest: Robinson ratified Moffat's treaty at Cape Town and it was made public. To the Transvaal and Portugal it meant that the British sphere now ran to the Zambezi. The concession-seekers saw it differently: whatever Lobengula granted from now on would have to pass the High Commissioner.
entries.source_note: Keppel-Jones, Rhodes and Rhodesia (1983), pp. 44–45, as cited in the Rudd Concession article (Military Wiki mirror); ratification date also in Zimbabwe Field Guide.

entries.headline: Three men leave Kimberley, nominally on a hunting trip
entries.digest: Rudd, Maguire and Thompson set out north from Kimberley with wagons, saying they were going hunting. At Shoshong the Bangwato ruler Khama held them up, and a letter from Robinson helped them through. Rival syndicates were also making for Bulawayo.
entries.source_note: Departure date in Zimbabwe Field Guide (Rudd Concession article) and in Ivon Fry's reminiscences page; Rudd's journal published 1949 (Gold and the Gospel in Mashonaland).

entries.place: Umvutcha, the royal kraal north of Bulawayo
entries.headline: Rudd's party reaches the king's kraal first
entries.digest: The party arrived at Lobengula's kraal and set up camp among other white petitioners already waiting on the king. For weeks they had audiences without result. Rudd's journal is the grantees' running account of these weeks.
entries.source_note: Galbraith, Crown and Charter (1974), p. 66, as cited (Military Wiki mirror); Zimbabwe Field Guide gives the same date.

entries.headline: The London syndicate's man arrives three weeks behind
entries.digest: Maund arrived for the Exploring Company syndicate, about three weeks after Rudd. He had been at the king's town on official business in 1885 and was liked there. Rather than racing Rudd for a signature, he became the companion of a different initiative: the king's wish to send his own men to see the Queen.
entries.source_note: Zimbabwe Field Guide (Rudd article: 'three weeks ahead of Maund'); Vaughn-Williams (1947) via Zimbabwe Field Guide node 602.

entries.headline: A British official rides in with an escort of police
entries.digest: Shippard arrived at the king's town with Major Hamilton Goold-Adams and sixteen Bechuanaland Border Police. The young warriors were reported to be alarmed by the uniformed escort. According to later accounts, Shippard told the king that Rhodes's party were the most trustworthy of the white men seeking concessions. He left before the signing.
entries.source_note: Rotberg, The Founder (1988), p. 260, as cited (Military Wiki mirror); escort and assurance from Vaughn-Williams (1947), as summarised in Zimbabwe Field Guide node 602. Exact day not established.

entries.headline: On an old brandy case, the king makes his mark
entries.digest: After a final morning session with the izinduna, the king sat on an old brandy case in the buck (goat) kraal. Rudd thought him anxious. For about half an hour Lobengula refused to sign, saying his promise was enough. Rudd asked Helm to hand over the paper, and the king made his mark. Rudd, Maguire and Thompson signed as grantees.
entries.source_note: Rudd's journal as summarised in Zimbabwe Field Guide (Rudd Concession article); final session and signing per Keppel-Jones (1983), pp. 77–78, as cited.

entries.headline: The missionary certifies that all was explained
entries.digest: Helm signed as a witness with J. F. Dreyer and wrote an endorsement, dated at the Umgusa River the same day. It certified that he had interpreted and explained the document to the king and his full council of izinduna and that the customs of the nation had been observed before the mark was made. Later he also confirmed that Rudd had made spoken assurances that are nowhere in the text.
entries.quote: has been fully interpreted and explained by me
entries.source_note: Endorsement text on SAHO, 'Rudd Concession by King Lobengula of Matabeleland (1888)'; place and date per Zimbabwe Field Guide; Helm's later confirmation per Keppel-Jones (1983), p. 77, as cited.

entries.headline: A private word with the king, then 'the epoch of our lives'
entries.digest: Thompson recalled that he and the councillor Lotshe spoke privately with the king just before he agreed. He wrote that he had promised gifts to Lotshe and to Sikombo if they helped. He remembered Maguire turning to him after the signing to say this was the great moment of their lives.
entries.source_note: Thompson, Matabele Thompson: An Autobiography (ed. Rouillard), as summarised in Zimbabwe Field Guide 'Matabele Thompson; his role in the Rudd Concession'; Maguire's remark per Keppel-Jones (1983), p. 78. Written decades later.

entries.place: The Kalahari edge, between Tati and Kimberley
entries.headline: Lost without water, Rudd hides the concession
entries.digest: Hurrying south by mule cart, Rudd lost the road and ran out of water. Believing he might die, he hid the signed concession and left a letter nearby saying where it was. A San camp found him and helped him on. Twenty days after leaving the kraal he reached Kimberley with the paper.
entries.source_note: Rudd's journal (published 1949) as summarised in Zimbabwe Field Guide; exact days of the ordeal not established.

entries.headline: An earlier concession-seeker dies as Rudd returns
entries.digest: Fry recalled that his father, J. L. Fry, a De Beers employee fluent in isiZulu whom Rhodes had sent earlier to seek a concession, had fallen ill at Bulawayo and died at Kimberley at about this time. Later, at the Kimberley Club, Rhodes told Ivon to bring him his agreement. Ivon came to believe his own attorney had sold it to Rhodes.
entries.source_note: Ivon Fry's reminiscences (recorded 1938 by Foster Windram), Zimbabwe Field Guide node 707.

entries.headline: The concession reaches Rhodes
entries.digest: Rudd arrived in Kimberley and handed the document to Rhodes. Two days later, on 21 November, he saw Robinson. Within the week the Cape newspapers carried an account of the grant.
entries.source_note: Keppel-Jones (1983), pp. 79–80, as cited; Zimbabwe Field Guide (Rudd article).

entries.headline: The Cape papers print the grant, without the rifles
entries.digest: The Cape Times and Cape Argus published an account of the concession that left out the 1,000 rifles and 100,000 rounds. It reached Robinson's desk in that form. On 5 December he wrote to the Colonial Office about the concession, and London later told Parliament he regarded it as advantageous on grounds of public policy.
entries.source_note: Keppel-Jones (1983), pp. 79–81, as cited (Military Wiki mirror); Hansard HC Deb 25 Feb 1889 for Robinson's view.

entries.headline: A royal notice warns concession-seekers away
entries.digest: Two days after the press reports, a notice in the king's name appeared in Cape Town. It warned concession-seekers to stay out of his country. The scribe who wrote it down at Bulawayo is not recorded in the sources used here.
entries.source_note: Keppel-Jones (1983), p. 81, as cited ('two days' after 24 Nov); Zimbabwe Field Guide gives c. 26 Nov 1888.

entries.date_display: late 1888 (sources vary from 1 November to mid-December)
entries.headline: The king sends his eyes to find the Queen
entries.digest: The king sent Mshete and Babayane south with Maund and Colenbrander, carrying a letter written down in English. It said he wanted to know whether there was a Queen, and that the izinduna were his eyes. If there was a Queen, he asked her to advise and help him and to send someone she trusted.
entries.source_note: Letter text as quoted in Zimbabwe Field Guide node 447; departure dates differ (Plaut 2016: 1 Nov; Field Guide: late Nov; Keppel-Jones: mid-Dec). The English was taken down by Maund.

entries.headline: Helm reads the real text against a trader's version
entries.digest: The trader William Tainton had been translating newspaper reports for the king and adding his own exaggerations of what the concession allowed. Helm read the actual text to Lobengula to show that Tainton's claims were not in it. This did not settle the matter: the king's complaint was about what he had been told, not only what was written.
entries.source_note: Zimbabwe Field Guide (Rudd article, citing Warhurst 1973).

entries.place: Bulawayo (printed in the Bechuanaland News and Malmani Chronicle)
entries.headline: The king suspends the concession pending his inquiry
entries.digest: A notice dated 18 January in Lobengula's name said that a concession granted to Rudd, Maguire and Thompson was under question. Until he had looked into it, all action under it was suspended. It was printed in the Bechuanaland News and the Malmani Chronicle on 2 February. In April it was read out in the House of Commons.
entries.quote: all action in respect of said concession is hereby suspended
entries.source_note: Date and wording as quoted by Labouchere, HC Deb 2 April 1889 (Hansard); publication date per Keppel-Jones (1983), p. 86, as cited.

entries.headline: The High Commissioner cables London about the king's envoys
entries.digest: Robinson telegraphed Lord Knutsford about the two izinduna. They had been kept waiting in Cape Town for about two weeks before being allowed to sail. That same day the king's suspension notice was appearing in the border newspapers.
entries.source_note: Zimbabwe Field Guide node 447 (citing Parsons).

entries.headline: A trader writes that the king disowns Rudd's paper
entries.digest: Fry remembered receiving a letter from the trader F. W. Usher at Bulawayo. It reported that the king had said Fry's father's claim was good and that he had granted no concession to Rudd's party. Fry then went back to Bulawayo to calm the traders' opposition, this time on Rhodes's side.
entries.source_note: Ivon Fry's reminiscences (1938), Zimbabwe Field Guide node 707.

entries.headline: The government has no opinion on its validity or merits
entries.digest: Charles Bradlaugh asked whether a concession from Lobengula to Rhodes, chairman of De Beers, or his agent Rudd had been sanctioned. De Worms described a grant of all the king's dominions except Tati, for an annuity and 1,000 rifles with 100,000 rounds. He said Shippard had been a hundred miles away and knew nothing of the talks. He added that the High Commissioner thought the grant advantageous, and that the government would express no opinion.
entries.quote: not consider it necessary to express any opinion
entries.source_note: Hansard, HC Deb 25 February 1889, 'South Africa — the De Beers mine'.

entries.headline: Two elderly izinduna land in England
entries.digest: Mshete and Babayane landed from the steamship Moor with Maund and Colenbrander. The British press treated them as a curiosity, and their names were printed in a variety of spellings. They had come to confirm with their own eyes what their king had been told.
entries.source_note: Plaut, 'Lobenguela's izinduna' (2016), via SAHO.

entries.headline: Maund interprets for the envoys before Lord Knutsford
entries.digest: At the Colonial Office the izinduna met the Colonial Secretary, Lord Knutsford, with Maund interpreting. Everything they said and heard therefore passed through the agent of a rival syndicate. The next day they were taken to Windsor.
entries.source_note: Plaut (2016), via SAHO.

entries.headline: The izinduna stand before the Queen
entries.digest: The two izinduna were received by Queen Victoria in St George's Hall, with fifty Life Guards in attendance. They had come to learn whether she existed and what she advised.
entries.source_note: Plaut (2016), via SAHO ('the following day' after 1 March); Zimbabwe Field Guide node 658 gives 2 March 1889.

entries.headline: A sovereign on a chain, inscribed to the king
entries.digest: The Queen's gift for Lobengula was a chain carrying an 1887 Jubilee five-pound piece, inscribed with her name, his and the month. It looked like gold but was in fact pinchbeck. When it reached Bulawayo the king was reported to dislike it, partly because its red case was thought unlucky.
entries.quote: From Queen Victoria to Lo Bengula. March 1889.
entries.source_note: Zimbabwe Field Guide node 658 (citing Summers, Rhodesiana Publication 26, 1972; South African Museum Annual Report 1912). Presentation day not separately recorded; placed with the audience.

entries.headline: Breakfast with the Aborigines' Protection Society
entries.digest: The Aborigines' Protection Society, which had campaigned against concession-mongering, gave the envoys breakfast. It handed them a letter for the king warning him against letting gold mining into his country. They were also shown Woolwich arsenal, the Bank of England's gold vaults, the zoo and Madame Tussaud's.
entries.source_note: Plaut (2016), via SAHO; Zimbabwe Field Guide node 658 for the sightseeing. Exact day of the breakfast not established.

entries.headline: 'The size of Italy': Chamberlain presses on the rifles
entries.digest: Joseph Chamberlain described the grant as covering a territory the size of Italy for a yearly payment and a thousand rifles. He asked whether the king would be warned about such a monopoly. De Worms said the government did not approve of the arms term and would advise Lobengula to have it altered. He also said the king, being independent, had only recently asked for advice.
entries.source_note: Hansard, HC Deb 11 March 1889, 'Matabaleland'.

entries.headline: Ten hours before the council of izinduna
entries.digest: On the day Chamberlain was raising the concession at Westminster, a great council of izinduna at Bulawayo began questioning Helm and Thompson about what had been signed. Thompson remembered being cross-examined for more than ten hours and living afterwards in fear for his life. He also remembered feeling he could not leave without endangering the concession.
entries.source_note: Date per Keppel-Jones (1983), p. 86; ten-hour interrogation per Davidson (1988), p. 140, both as cited; Thompson's feelings per his autobiography (Zimbabwe Field Guide).

entries.headline: The interpreter is questioned by the council
entries.digest: Helm was summoned with Thompson before the izinduna. As the certifying interpreter, he was asked to account for what the king had been told the paper contained. Suspicion that the missionary had served the grantees outlasted the inquiry.
entries.source_note: Zimbabwe Field Guide (Rudd article): 'an izinDuna council questioned Helm and Thompson', 11 March 1889. The substance of Helm's answers is not detailed in the sources used.

entries.headline: Ten thousand soldiers on parade for the king's eyes
entries.digest: The envoys were taken to Aldershot to watch about 10,000 troops at a review, and to see the guns at Shoeburyness and the dockyards. The display was meant to impress on them the power behind the Queen. The Illustrated London News reported the visit on 16 March.
entries.source_note: Plaut (2016), via SAHO (press dates 16 March, Illustrated London News; 26 March, Daily Telegraph).

entries.headline: What the envoys came for, as the government reports it
entries.digest: Asked whether the envoys had a special mission, de Worms said they had come to learn about the Queen and her country and to seek protection against foreign invasion. He said they also sought advice about white men who had come to dig for gold. The king, he said, would be told not to grant concessions without careful consideration and not to give any individual a monopoly.
entries.source_note: Hansard, HC Deb 15 March 1889, 'King Lo Bengula'.

entries.place: Colonial Office, London (in the Queen's name)
entries.headline: An ox, not the whole herd
entries.digest: The reply sent in the Queen's name said she had heard the king's words and was glad to receive his messengers. She advised him not to grant concessions of land or leave to dig hastily, and to consider every request carefully. It also told him that the High Commissioner was her officer and had her full trust.
entries.quote: A King gives a stranger an ox, not his whole herd
entries.source_note: Text of Knutsford's letter of 26 March 1889 as quoted in Zimbabwe Field Guide node 447 (citing Parsons and the Blue Book correspondence).

entries.headline: No power to confirm or disallow
entries.digest: On the day the Queen's letter was dated, Henry Labouchere asked whether representations could be made to the envoys. De Worms replied that the government had neither approved the Rudd concession nor had any power to confirm or disallow concessions in Matabeleland. He noted the armed steamer clause and the £500 alternative.
entries.quote: no power to make any representation
entries.source_note: Hansard, HC Deb 26 March 1889, 'Lo Bengula'.

entries.headline: The king's notice is read aloud at Westminster
entries.digest: Labouchere read Lobengula's notice of 18 January into the record and asked whether the king had disowned the concession. De Worms said there was no official information. He suggested the announcement might have come from Rudd's rivals. He said Britain could advise within its sphere of influence but could not prevent a ruler from granting concessions, and outlined a plan to bring all valid concessions under one control.
entries.source_note: Hansard, HC Deb 2 April 1889, 'Lo Bengula's concessions'.

entries.headline: 'Neither my words nor the words of those who got it'
entries.digest: In a letter to the Queen, written down for him in English, the king told the story as he saw it. Men led by Rudd had asked for a place to dig for gold, offering certain things in return. A paper was put before him, he asked what it contained, and he was told it held his words and theirs. He put his hand to it. Months later, he said, it was shown to him that he had signed away the mineral rights of his whole country. He and his izinduna would not recognise the paper.
entries.quote: contains neither my words nor the words of those who got it
entries.source_note: C.5918 (1890), enclosure in no. 101, as cited by Cary, 'Jameson and Lobengula'; text reprinted in E. D. Morel, The Black Man's Burden (1920), pp. 34–35. Early April refusal of the rifles per Rotberg (1988), p. 269.

entries.headline: Home with the Queen's words and a chain
entries.digest: Mshete and Babayane returned to the king's kraal and delivered Knutsford's letter and the Queen's gift, along with what they had seen with their own eyes. Their report reached a council still divided over the concession.
entries.source_note: Zimbabwe Field Guide nodes 447 and 658; Rotberg (1988), p. 271, as cited.

entries.headline: A nineteen-year-old is asked what he wants
entries.digest: Vaughn-Williams and his brother arrived and stayed nearly three months. He remembered the king asking at their first meeting what they wanted from him, the question every white visitor was met with that year. He judged Lobengula to be about fifty-six and thought him dignified and commanding.
entries.source_note: Vaughn-Williams, A Visit to Lobengula in 1889 (1947), as summarised in Zimbabwe Field Guide node 602.

entries.headline: Thanks for the Queen's word, but no officer wanted
entries.digest: In a letter sent through Shippard, the king thanked the Queen for the message his izinduna had brought by mouth. He declined her offer to send an officer to live with him, saying he would ask for one if he found himself in need. The letter had not reached London when the next royal reply was drafted.
entries.quote: I do not need an officer to be sent.
entries.source_note: Letter of 10 August 1889 as quoted in Zimbabwe Field Guide node 447; its late arrival in London per Cary, 'Jameson and Lobengula', and Rotberg (1988), p. 271, as cited.

entries.headline: The assistant commissioner reports on a tense town
entries.digest: Moffat wrote to Shippard from Bulawayo in the weeks after the envoys' return, while the council's dispute over the concession was unresolved. His report went into the Blue Book London laid before Parliament in 1890.
entries.source_note: Moffat to Shippard, 28 August 1889, C.5918 no. 131, as cited by Cary, 'Jameson and Lobengula'. Content summarised only in general terms here.

entries.headline: After a great indaba, Lotshe is put to death
entries.digest: Vaughn-Williams recalled a large council in mid-September, after which Lotshe Hlabangana was put to death and his homestead destroyed. Lotshe was the senior councillor blamed for advising the king to accept the rifles and the paper. He remembered that many people of Lotshe's household were killed, about 300 by his reckoning.
entries.source_note: Vaughn-Williams (1947), as summarised in Zimbabwe Field Guide node 602; 'September 1889' for Lotshe's death per Cary, 'Jameson and Lobengula'.

entries.headline: Thompson rides for the border
entries.digest: Thompson recalled that after the killings he fled, riding and then walking to Tati, and going on by Shoshong to Mafeking. He returned later with Leander Starr Jameson. Ivon Fry's recollections, set down in 1938, dispute several details of Thompson's account of these days.
entries.source_note: Thompson, Autobiography, as summarised in Zimbabwe Field Guide 'Matabele Thompson'; Fry's dissent per node 707.

entries.headline: The king reads the flight as distrust
entries.digest: Vaughn-Williams remembered the king's reaction to Thompson's flight: he took it to show that Thompson did not trust him. He threatened to cancel the concession unless Thompson came back. In this memory, the king treated the concession as a bond of personal trust between men.
entries.source_note: Vaughn-Williams (1947), via Zimbabwe Field Guide nodes 602 and 607.

entries.headline: The original paper is laid beside the copy
entries.digest: At his first meeting with Jameson, Rhodes's envoy, the king had the original concession produced and compared with the copy. Eleven days later in London, on 29 October, the royal charter of the British South Africa Company was granted, resting on that paper. The izinduna said they would return the original soon. Two months later it still had not come back.
entries.source_note: Cary, 'Jameson and Lobengula, 1889–90' (citing Jameson's letters to Harris); charter date per Rotberg (1988), pp. 284–285, as cited.

entries.headline: The Company will trust the king's word of mouth
entries.digest: Helm wrote to the LMS secretary, Wardlaw Thompson. Jameson had sent him to tell the king that the Company would rely entirely on his spoken word. A year after the dispute over spoken and written terms, the Company was now promising to rely on the king's word alone.
entries.source_note: Helm to W. Thompson, 20 December 1889, LMS archives LO6/1/5, as cited by Cary, 'Jameson and Lobengula'.

entries.headline: Epilogue: the king refuses the monthly payment
entries.digest: After the Fort Victoria clash with the Company in July, the king refused to take the monthly £100 paid under the concession, saying it was paid for his blood. The next day Jameson made a secret agreement at Fort Victoria with volunteers for a war against him. The columns moved in October.
entries.source_note: Millin, Rhodes (1952 ed.), p. 191, as cited (Military Wiki mirror). Exact form of the king's words survives only as reported.

entries.place: Bulawayo and the country to the north
entries.headline: Epilogue: the king's stockade burns and the cattle go
entries.digest: Ndansi Kumalo told Perham that the king had not wanted war and had sent his regiments away. He said the fighting at the Shangani and Bembezi went against the amaNdebele. The white forces entered Bulawayo and the king's enclosure was burned as he fled. Most of the cattle passed into white hands, and the chiefs were told to give up their weapons, which they did. Lobengula died in the north in January 1894.
entries.source_note: Ndansi Kumalo in Perham, Ten Africans (1936), as reprinted in Macmillan sources reader; Bulawayo set on fire 3 November 1893 per Ranger (2010), as cited.

entries.headline: Babayane tells his London story to Rhodes's camp
entries.digest: Seven years after Windsor, during the 1896 rising, Babayane was reported telling the story of his journey to London at Rhodes's camp. By then the kingdom whose eyes he had been had fallen.
entries.source_note: Zimbabwe Field Guide node 447 ('1896: Babayane tells his London story to Rhodes's camp'). The original reporter is not identified in the sources used.

convergences.label: The signing at Umvutcha
convergences.note: Rudd records a hesitant king on a brandy case and a paper handed across by the missionary. Helm certifies that everything was explained, yet later confirms that spoken promises were left out. Thompson remembers private persuasion and promised gifts. The king's own account of this day arrives only in April 1889, through a scribe.

convergences.label: The paper reaches the Cape, without its rifles
convergences.note: In one week the concession reaches Rhodes, appears in the Cape press without the arms clause, lands on the High Commissioner's desk, and is answered by a royal notice warning seekers away. Meanwhile Fry's father, an earlier seeker, dies in Kimberley.

convergences.label: Suspension notice and the envoys' delay
convergences.note: As Helm reads the true text to the king to correct a trader's version, the king dictates his suspension. Robinson is cabling London about envoys held at Cape Town, and Fry hears from Bulawayo that the king disowns Rudd.

convergences.label: Windsor
convergences.note: The izinduna see the Queen; a pinchbeck chain is given in her name; Maund, the rival agent, interprets the day before. Each records a different exchange: confirmation, condescending gift-giving, and commercial opportunity.

convergences.label: Westminster and Bulawayo on the same Monday
convergences.note: In the Commons Chamberlain calls the grant 'the size of Italy' and the government disowns the rifle clause. At Bulawayo the izinduna begin hours of questioning of the grantee and the interpreter. Neither gathering knew of the other.

convergences.label: The ox and the herd
convergences.note: The letter dated in the Queen's name advises the king to give a stranger an ox, not the herd, and to trust the High Commissioner. The same day, the government tells the Commons it has no power to confirm or disallow concessions. The envoys, still touring, carry the first message home.

convergences.label: Repudiation in two capitals
convergences.note: Three weeks after his January notice is read aloud at Westminster and called possibly a rivals' forgery, the king dictates his fullest account: the paper holds neither his words nor theirs.

convergences.label: Lotshe's death and Thompson's flight
convergences.note: A young visitor, the fleeing grantee and a rival agent all remember the September crisis, and they disagree on its details. The king's reaction, as remembered, was to treat the concession as a matter of personal trust.

ties.note: Fellow grantees who travelled from Kimberley together and signed side by side on 30 October 1888.
Negotiated over five weeks at Umvutcha. The grant bears Rudd's name and the king's mark.
Helm had lived near the king's town since 1875 and interpreted the concession to him. He read him the text again in January 1889.
Helm witnessed Rudd's concession and certified it. He later confirmed spoken promises by Rudd that the text omits.
Questioned together before the council of izinduna from 11 March 1889. Thompson visited the Helms shortly before he fled.
Moffat obtained the king's mark on the February 1888 treaty and stayed at Bulawayo as the Crown's officer.
Shippard visited in mid-October 1888 with an armed escort and is reported to have spoken for Rhodes's party.
Senior izinduna of the king's council, sent as his 'eyes' and returning with the Queen's message in August 1889.
Maund escorted the izinduna from Bulawayo to London and back and interpreted for them at the Colonial Office.
Letters crossed between them: the king's letter carried by the envoys, the reply of 26 March 1889, the king's letters of 23 April and 10 August 1889.
Both worked for Rhodes, but Fry's 1938 reminiscences dispute Thompson's memoir on Lotshe's death and on the flight.
A guest at the royal kraal from August to October 1889.
An amaNdebele subject of the king who decades later played him on film and told Perham the king had not wanted war.

claims.claim: Lobengula will make no treaty with, or cession to, any foreign power without the High Commissioner's sanction.
claims.evidence: Moffat treaty, ratified at Cape Town 25 April 1888 (Keppel-Jones; Zimbabwe Field Guide)

claims.claim: The king grants 'complete and exclusive charge over all metals and minerals' in his kingdoms, with power to exclude others.
In return: £100 each lunar month, 1,000 Martini-Henry rifles, 100,000 rounds, and a Zambezi steamboat or £500.
The document was fully interpreted and explained to the king and his full council, and customary usages were observed.
Spoken assurances were given beyond the text: no more than ten white men, no digging near towns, obedience to the king's laws.
claims.evidence: Helm's later confirmation, as cited by Keppel-Jones (1983), p. 77; Zimbabwe Field Guide

claims.claim: Gifts were promised to the councillors Lotshe and Sikombo if they helped the concession through.
claims.evidence: Thompson, Autobiography (memoir), via Zimbabwe Field Guide

claims.claim: The king wishes to know if there is a Queen, and asks her to advise and help him; the izinduna are his eyes.
claims.evidence: Letter carried by the envoys, taken down by Maund (Zimbabwe Field Guide node 447)

claims.claim: All action under the concession is suspended pending the king's investigation.
claims.evidence: Bechuanaland News notice, quoted in Hansard 2 April 1889

claims.claim: The government expresses no opinion on the concession's validity or merits; the High Commissioner thinks it advantageous.
The government does not approve the arms term and will advise the king to have it altered.
The envoys came to learn about the Queen and to seek protection against foreign invasion, and advice about gold-seekers.
claims.evidence: As reported by the Under-Secretary, Hansard 15 March 1889

claims.claim: Do not grant concessions of land or leave to dig hastily; 'a King gives a stranger an ox, not his whole herd'; trust the High Commissioner.
claims.evidence: Knutsford's letter in the Queen's name (Zimbabwe Field Guide node 447; Blue Book correspondence)

claims.claim: The Aborigines' Protection Society warns the king, by letter, against allowing gold mining.
The king and his izinduna will not recognise the paper; it contains neither his words nor the words of those who got it.
The king thanks the Queen for her spoken word but needs no officer sent; he will ask if pressed.
claims.evidence: Letter via Shippard (Zimbabwe Field Guide node 447)

claims.claim: The Company will trust entirely to the king's word of mouth.
claims.evidence: Helm to W. Thompson, LMS LO6/1/5, cited by Cary

threads_out.note: The Berlin General Act's rules on notification and effective authority set off the concession-hunting of the late 1880s. In the Commons on 2 April 1889 MPs pressed de Worms on what Britain's declared 'sphere of influence' over Lobengula's country meant, and the Moffat treaty had been the instrument for claiming that sphere against Portugal and the Transvaal.

The Rudd party's hopes rested on the Witwatersrand finds of 1886. Rhodes's and Rudd's Gold Fields of South Africa was a Rand company, and the dream of a 'second Rand' north of the Limpopo drove the race to Bulawayo. A rival claim to the concession was settled with the Leask group in Johannesburg in January 1889.

Rudd was Rhodes's partner in the Kimberley diamond fields and in De Beers. The party set out from Kimberley on 15 August 1888 and brought the signed paper back there on 19 November. Bradlaugh's Commons question of 25 February 1889 named Rhodes as chairman of the De Beers mine.

As at Waitangi, the meaning of the Rudd agreement turned on the gap between the text and what was explained aloud by a missionary interpreter. Helm's certificate and his later admission of unwritten promises match the dispute over Henry Williams's translation and the spoken assurances given in 1840.
